title: Methods
text:
The experiment is located in the Jackson Demonstration State Forest in coastal northern California. Four harvest treatments were replicated at four sites in 2012: group selection (GS), high-density dispersed retention (HD), high-density aggregated retention (HA), and low-density dispersed retention (LD). The retained-overstory treatments targeted post-harvest relative densities of 13% or 21%; group selection created a 1-ha opening with a lightly thinned buffer. These treatments were designed to examine alternative pathways for developing multiaged redwood stands (Berrill & O’Hara, 2009; Reineke, 1933).
Ten years after harvest, regeneration plots and fuel transects were established within each 0.2-ha treatment macro plot. Regeneration measurements characterized redwood, tanoak, and Douglas-fir; fuel transects characterized dead surface fuels and live vegetation. The plots were remeasured after precommercial thinning, which released selected conifers from competing trees and shrubs.



Detailed sampling procedures, model diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses will be retained as supplementary material.


Basal area was modeled separately for redwood, tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species using zero-inflated Gamma mixed models with a conditional log link. Treatment was a fixed effect; site and macro plot nested within site were random intercepts. Each species category had its own intercept-only zero and dispersion components. Each model used 64 vegetation-plot observations from four sites and 16 macro plots. Arithmetic mean basal area included modeled zeros and integrated over both fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. Confidence intervals for the means were calculated using the log-scale delta method with the full parameter covariance, including random-effect variance uncertainty. Redwood and tanoak estimates are displayed in the Results; estimates for all four categories are reported in the supplement.



Reported values are model-based arithmetic mean loads, including modeled zeros and integrating over fitted random effects, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts.
These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

title: Discussion
text:
Discussion
The discussion will first interpret regeneration responses in relation to the silvicultural objective of developing a new redwood cohort beneath varying levels of retained overstory. It will then interpret phase-specific fuel conditions and the PCT-associated contrast as a linked management question, with conclusions limited to the reviewed sampling design and analysis.
This structure treats silviculture and fire management as linked management questions while keeping conclusions within the support of the reviewed analyses and cited literature.

title: Abstract
text:
Abstract
Forest managers using retention forestry need information on regeneration and fuel development to design productive stands in fire-adapted ecosystems. We analyzed 10-year remeasurement data from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment in Jackson Demonstration State Forest, California. The experiment compared group selection, aggregated retention, and low- and high-density dispersed retention treatments and measured regeneration, sprout growth, and surface fuel loading.
Redwood regeneration responded strongly to increasing canopy openness, whereas tanoak responses were more modest. Sprout-height findings will remain part of the main regeneration evidence. Fuel measurements describe conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including the PCT-associated contrast. The manuscript will evaluate how overstory retention affects regeneration while presenting fuel components in a form useful for integrated silviculture, fuels, and fire management.

Selected analysis and manuscript outputs
The selected manuscript analysis fits all four species categories separately: ba_ha ~ treat + (1 | site/treat), ziGamma(log), zero ~1, dispersion ~1. 05-fit-selected-species-models.R produces these outputs. Each category has 64 observations, four site groups, and 16 nested macro-plot groups. The plot-level random effect is omitted. Selection follows the user’s biological modeling decision rather than the minimum-AIC alternative.
Current outputs are under outputs/regeneration/selected-species-models/: 16 integrated means and full-covariance intervals, four fitted models, fit and variance registers, DHARMa plots/tests, optimizer checks, and provenance. All four models are checked against BFGS; all 16 means are verified using model predictions, numerical gradients, and quadrature. RW/TO means reproduce script 03’s species fits. The script protects the thesis input and historical joint reference outputs with checksums.


Historical joint-model reference
01-generate-rd02-display.R reads exported historical estimates and audit tables, then generates the reference display. The original mba replay, prediction, gradient, and quadrature checks execute in analysis/scripts/export-publication-inputs.R under thesis R and renv. Publication never loads analysis/regen_visualize.rda. The selected model is m5 from analysis/analysis/regen_visualize.qmd: zero-inflated Gamma, conditional log link, ba_ha ~ treat * spp + (1 | site:spp), zero and dispersion formulas ~spp. All four species classes remain in the fit. Only redwood and tanoak enter the main display. This is basal area per hectare, not stem density.
For species g and treatment t, the integrated expectation is (1 - p_zero[g]) * exp(X[t,g] beta + sigma_site:spp^2 / 2). There are no random effects in the zero component. Gamma dispersion needs no lognormal residual correction. Four site rows receive equal weights, but the integrated expectations coincide because site is not a fixed predictor. This is the same arithmetic-response estimand used for RD04, audited here for the regeneration model’s distinct structure.
The full sdr$cov.fixed covariance propagates uncertainty in conditional and zero coefficients and the log random-effect SD, including cross-covariances. Means use positive 95% log-scale delta-method intervals. Model-selection, measurement/aggregation, and model-structure uncertainty are not included. The retained site-by-species intercept does not explicitly model macro-plot clustering, unlike the fuel hierarchy. That design question remains open for scientific review; this script does not silently replace the thesis model.
Outputs in publication/outputs/regeneration/:

figures/rd02-regeneration-basal-area.png and .pdf: shared-scale historical display.
tables/rd02-basal-area-model-estimates.csv: all 16 species/treatment means.
tables/rd02-observed-basal-area-summary.csv: observed counts, zeros, and means.
inference-audit/: four-site grid and zero-effect/integrated comparison.
manifests/: input/script checksums, model specification, review status, session.

The thesis export operation checks all 16 historical cells against predict() and marginaleffects for the zero-effect reference, and against marginaleffects::hypotheses() for integrated means and SEs. Independent numerical gradients and numerical quadrature verify the analytic derivatives and integration factor. Export checksums are checked before publication execution and again at completion. No significance arrows, inherited p-values, or claims based on CI overlap are generated. Refitted bootstrap intervals remain possible later modeling work.


Full nested design comparison
02-compare-rd02-random-effects.R refits three models on the same 256 saved species/vegetation-plot rows:

Thesis: ba_ha ~ treat * spp + (1 | site:spp).
Full design: ba_ha ~ treat * spp + (1 | site/treat/plot).
Sensitivity: full design plus (1 | site:spp).

The full design expands to site, site:treatment (macro plot), and site:treatment:plot (vegetation plot) intercepts: 4, 16, and 64 groups. Plot/corner codes are reused and are not treated as globally unique IDs. All candidates use zero-inflated Gamma with conditional log link, the same treat*spp fixed effects, and ~spp zero and dispersion formulas. No random effects are added to the zero model. The sensitivity candidate distinguishes adding design clustering from removing species-specific site variation.
Outputs are in outputs/regeneration/random-effects-comparison/: ML fit/AIC/BIC/convergence records, variance components, row/grouped DHARMa tests and plots, integrated means and full-covariance delta-method intervals, optimizer and residual-tail sensitivity checks, and a model-comparison figure. The two primary covariance structures are not nested in one another; the comparison does not report an ordinary likelihood-ratio test. Lower AIC alone does not settle the scientific adequacy of a covariance structure.
The comparison checks refitted thesis likelihood against the saved fit, prediction matrices against predict(), and all integrated-mean gradients against numerical derivatives. It checks design-candidate optima using BFGS from initial random SDs of 0.3, alongside the main nlminb fits. Near-zero variance components are recorded rather than silently dropped. Their delta-method intervals are approximate near the boundary; no refitted bootstrap intervals are claimed.
DHARMa uses 1,000 unconditional simulations per model (seed 20261030), with recalculated residuals at site, macro-plot, and vegetation-plot levels. These checks are exploratory, not proof of independence; four sites provide little power at the site level. The baseline tail flag is checked again with 10,000 simulations and a different seed; flagged rows from both runs are retained. All observations remain in the fits.
The original thesis input and current lead figure/estimates are checksum protected. Fitted models and simulations remain local RDS artifacts. The comparison is recorded in publication/sections/rd02-random-effects-review.qmd, included in the RD02 workflow card. It does not automatically replace the lead model.


Separate RW and TO models with site and macro-plot effects
03-compare-rd02-separate-species.R gives each focal species ba_ha ~ treat + (1 | site/treat), with ziGamma(log), zero ~1, and dispersion ~1. There are 64 observations, 4 sites, 16 macro plots, and 64 vegetation plots per species. Each fit estimates its own variance components. Within one species, site-by-species is simply site. The plot-level random intercept is omitted; each species has one observation per vegetation plot.
For a valid AIC comparison, all three joint alternatives are refitted on the same 128 RW/TO rows. The separate pair’s log likelihoods and parameter counts are summed under species independence. Neither individual-species AICs nor the paired AIC are compared with the earlier 256-row, four-species AICs. Cross-species covariance is not estimated by the independent fits.
Outputs are in outputs/regeneration/separate-species-comparison/: fit and variance registers, same-data AIC comparison, 1,000-simulation DHARMa checks and treatment plots, full-covariance integrated means and intervals, BFGS/start sensitivity checks, provenance, session, and a comparison figure. All 32 mean cells are checked using predict(), numerical gradients, and quadrature. Original inputs and lead figure/estimates are checksum protected. The workflow includes publication/sections/rd02-separate-species-review.qmd. The script does not replace the lead model or generate significance arrows.


Overall sensitivity figures and tables
04-assemble-rd02-sensitivity.R reads their generated CSVs without refitting models or recalculating inference. The overall collection includes the three four-species joint fits, three RW/TO joint refits, the separate site/macro-plot RW/TO pair, and the selected four-category separate models.
outputs/regeneration/overall-sensitivity/ contains a four-panel figure (fitting-data scopes in rows, species in columns), an eight-configuration fit table, all 28 variance-component rows, 48 row-level diagnostic tests, and 96 complete mean/interval cells (64 focal-species cells in the figure). The separate species share a figure label; component_model_id preserves their individual fits. AIC differences are calculated within each data scope, never across the 256-row and 128-row groups.
The assembler checks that every source estimate and interval limit is copied exactly, all configuration/treatment/species cells are present once, AIC matches its log likelihood and parameter count, and source hashes are unchanged. The overall and focused species figures remain in the workflow with one fit comparison table. Full estimates, variance components, and diagnostics are downloads; duplicate rendered tables are omitted. Review prose summarizes treatment patterns, notable variance/interval differences, and diagnostic trends.

title: F01 — fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
01 — Derive components and audit pairing
Purpose. Separate reportable fuel components and construct matched transect records.
Rationale. Partition pre-PCT forest floor with Finney–Martin model 3, bound negative shallow litter extrapolations at zero, keep woody/herbaceous cover-height loads separate, and carry exported deadwood loads forward unchanged. Omit post-PCT litter/duff; standing woody reduction is potential contribution, not measured slash.


Calculation — f01-01-derive-components


task_begin("F01")
source("scripts/fuel/00-fuel-config.R")
task_progress("f01-01-derive-components")
local({
# Finney and Martin (1993), model 3: cumulative forest-floor mass (Mg ha^-1)
# from the surface to depth ds_cm within a profile of total depth dp_cm.
# The model is used only for the pre-PCT forest-floor measurements, where the
# recorded total depth and estimated litter proportion describe the forest floor.
# Its fitted range does not support a negative cumulative mass; the derivation
# script records and bounds such rare shallow-layer extrapolations at zero.
finney_martin_cumulative_load <- function(ds_cm, dp_cm) {
  result <- 6.461 * ds_cm^1.07 - 0.254 * dp_cm
  result[ds_cm == 0] <- 0
  result
}

publication_root <- .publication_render$root
script_dir <- file.path(publication_root, "scripts", "fuel")
paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)

paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
dir.create(paths$data, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(paths$manifests, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Typed, checksum-validated exports from the separate thesis operation.
transects <- readRDS(paths$input)
legacy_total_load <- readRDS(paths$legacy_load_input)
ids <- publication_fuel_ids

# Keep the field measurements intact for audit. Post-PCT forest-floor values
# are retained here but deliberately receive no duff/litter load conversion.
forest_floor_station <- transects |>
  select(phase, all_of(ids), matches("^(duff_litter|pct_litter|fbd)[12]$")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^(duff_litter|pct_litter|fbd)[12]$"),
    names_to = c(".value", "station"),
    names_pattern = "(.*?)([12])$"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    phase,
    across(all_of(ids)),
    station = as.integer(station),
    total_forest_floor_depth_cm = duff_litter,
    estimated_litter_fraction = pct_litter / 100,
    estimated_litter_depth_cm = total_forest_floor_depth_cm * estimated_litter_fraction,
    estimated_duff_depth_cm = total_forest_floor_depth_cm - estimated_litter_depth_cm,
    fuel_bed_depth_cm = fbd,
    forest_floor_load_eligible = phase == "prepct"
  )

if (any(forest_floor_station$estimated_litter_fraction < 0 |
  forest_floor_station$estimated_litter_fraction > 1, na.rm = TRUE)) {
  stop("Estimated litter fractions fall outside [0, 1].")
}

# Finney and Martin's cumulative curve partitions the pre-PCT total profile at
# the estimated litter/duff boundary. These are model-derived loads, not direct
# independent bulk-density measurements of the two layers.
forest_floor_pre_station <- forest_floor_station |>
  filter(forest_floor_load_eligible) |>
  mutate(
    total_forest_floor_load_mgha = finney_martin_cumulative_load(
      total_forest_floor_depth_cm,
      total_forest_floor_depth_cm
    ),
    litter_load_mgha = finney_martin_cumulative_load(
      estimated_litter_depth_cm,
      total_forest_floor_depth_cm
    ),
    litter_load_raw_mgha = litter_load_mgha,
    litter_load_bounded_at_zero = litter_load_raw_mgha < 0,
    litter_load_mgha = pmax(litter_load_raw_mgha, 0),
    duff_load_mgha = total_forest_floor_load_mgha - litter_load_mgha
  )

if (any(forest_floor_pre_station$duff_load_mgha < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
  stop("Finney-Martin component calculation produced a negative duff load; inspect the input depths before proceeding.")
}

forest_floor_components <- forest_floor_pre_station |>
  select(phase, all_of(ids), station, litter_load_mgha, duff_load_mgha) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with("_load_mgha"),
    names_to = "component",
    values_to = "load_mgha"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    component = recode(
      component,
      litter_load_mgha = "litter",
      duff_load_mgha = "duff"
    ),
    derivation = "Finney-Martin 1993 model 3 cumulative-load partition"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    load_mgha = mean(load_mgha),
    n_stations = sum(!is.na(load_mgha)),
    derivation = first(derivation),
    .by = c(all_of(ids), "phase", "component")
  )

# FireMon-style vegetation calculations remain separate by physiognomic class.
vegetation_station <- transects |>
  select(
    phase,
    all_of(ids),
    matches("^(live_woody|dead_woody|avg_w_ht|live_herb|dead_herb|avg_h_ht)[12]$")
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(phase, all_of(ids)),
    names_to = c(".value", "station"),
    names_pattern = "(.*?)([12])$"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    woody_height_m = if_else(live_woody == 0 & dead_woody == 0, 0, avg_w_ht),
    herb_height_m = if_else(live_herb == 0 & dead_herb == 0, 0, avg_h_ht),
    woody_load_mgha = ((live_woody + dead_woody) / 100) * woody_height_m * 18,
    herb_load_mgha = ((live_herb + dead_herb) / 100) * herb_height_m * 8
  ) |>
  select(phase, all_of(ids), station, woody_load_mgha, herb_load_mgha)

vegetation_components <- vegetation_station |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with("_load_mgha"),
    names_to = "component",
    values_to = "load_mgha"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    component = recode(
      component,
      woody_load_mgha = "woody_vegetation",
      herb_load_mgha = "herbaceous_vegetation"
    ),
    derivation = "FireMon cover-height bulk-density calculation retained by component"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    load_mgha = mean(load_mgha),
    n_stations = sum(!is.na(load_mgha)),
    derivation = first(derivation),
    .by = c("phase", all_of(ids), "component")
  )

dead_woody_components <- legacy_total_load |>
  select(phase, all_of(ids), onehr, tenhr, hundhr, thoushr) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(onehr, tenhr, hundhr, thoushr),
    names_to = "component",
    values_to = "load_mgha"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    derivation = "Unchanged thesis-era dead-woody load carried forward from calculate_fuel_load.rda"
  )

# Phase comes from the identifiers retained above. Restrict the exported long
# component table to reportable component/phase combinations.
fuel_components_transect <- bind_rows(
  forest_floor_components,
  vegetation_components,
  dead_woody_components
) |>
  mutate(
    component = factor(
      component,
      levels = c("litter", "duff", "onehr", "tenhr", "hundhr", "thoushr", "woody_vegetation", "herbaceous_vegetation")
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(phase, site, treatment, corner, azi, component)

# Explicit pre/post joins replace the thesis-era lexical phase ordering used to
# construct veg_diff. The primary PCT contrast is woody standing vegetation
# reduction; it is an inferred surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load.
vegetation_wide <- fuel_components_transect |>
  filter(component %in% c("woody_vegetation", "herbaceous_vegetation")) |>
  select(all_of(ids), phase, component, load_mgha) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = c(component, phase),
    values_from = load_mgha,
    names_sep = "_"
  )

fuel_bed_depth_phase <- forest_floor_station |>
  summarise(
    fuel_bed_depth_cm = mean(fuel_bed_depth_cm),
    n_fuel_bed_stations = sum(!is.na(fuel_bed_depth_cm)),
    .by = c("phase", all_of(ids))
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = phase,
    values_from = c(fuel_bed_depth_cm, n_fuel_bed_stations),
    names_sep = "_"
  )

fuel_paired_transect <- vegetation_wide |>
  filter(
    !is.na(woody_vegetation_prepct),
    !is.na(woody_vegetation_postpct)
  ) |>
  inner_join(fuel_bed_depth_phase, by = ids) |>
  mutate(
    woody_standing_reduction_mgha = woody_vegetation_prepct - woody_vegetation_postpct,
    herbaceous_vegetation_change_mgha = herbaceous_vegetation_postpct - herbaceous_vegetation_prepct,
    interpretation = "Woody standing-vegetation reduction is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution; it is not a direct slash-load measurement."
  )

pairing_qc <- bind_rows(
  transmute(distinct(filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_prepct)), across(all_of(ids))), status = "pre-PCT woody observation"),
  transmute(distinct(filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_postpct)), across(all_of(ids))), status = "post-PCT woody observation"),
  transmute(anti_join(
    distinct(filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_prepct)), across(all_of(ids))),
    distinct(filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_postpct)), across(all_of(ids))),
    by = ids
  ), status = "pre-PCT woody observation without post-PCT match"),
  transmute(anti_join(
    distinct(filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_postpct)), across(all_of(ids))),
    distinct(filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_prepct)), across(all_of(ids))),
    by = ids
  ), status = "post-PCT woody observation without pre-PCT match"),
  transmute(distinct(fuel_paired_transect, across(all_of(ids))), status = "matched woody pair")
) |>
  count(status, name = "n_transects")

data_dictionary <- tibble(
  component = c("litter", "duff", "woody_vegetation", "herbaceous_vegetation", "woody_standing_reduction_mgha", "fuel_bed_depth_cm"),
  unit = c("Mg ha^-1", "Mg ha^-1", "Mg ha^-1", "Mg ha^-1", "Mg ha^-1", "cm"),
  reporting_phase = c("pre-PCT only", "pre-PCT only", "pre-PCT and post-PCT", "pre-PCT and post-PCT", "matched pre/post", "measurement retained for protocol review"),
  definition = c(
    "Model-derived upper forest-floor load using Finney-Martin cumulative model 3 and the estimated litter-depth boundary. Negative shallow-layer extrapolations are bounded at zero and retained in the station-level audit output.",
    "Model-derived lower forest-floor load: total Finney-Martin forest-floor load minus modeled litter load. Two shallow estimated litter layers were bounded at zero after the equation returned negative mass.",
    "FireMon-style cover-height estimate using the existing woody bulk-density constant.",
    "FireMon-style cover-height estimate using the existing herbaceous bulk-density constant.",
    "Pre-PCT minus post-PCT woody standing vegetation; inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load.",
    "Recorded field value; do not interpret as slash depth until protocol comparability is confirmed."
  )
)

saveRDS(forest_floor_station, file.path(paths$data, "forest-floor-measurements-station.rds"))
saveRDS(forest_floor_pre_station, file.path(paths$data, "forest-floor-pre-components-station.rds"))
saveRDS(fuel_components_transect, file.path(paths$data, "fuel-components-transect.rds"))
saveRDS(fuel_paired_transect, file.path(paths$data, "fuel-paired-transect.rds"))
write_csv(pairing_qc, file.path(paths$data, "fuel-pairing-qc.csv"))
write_csv(data_dictionary, file.path(paths$data, "fuel-component-data-dictionary.csv"))

provenance_lines <- c(
  "input: publication/inputs/thesis/fuel-measurements.rds",
  "legacy-dead-woody-input: publication/inputs/thesis/fuel-deadwood-loads.rds",
  "export_manifest: publication/inputs/thesis/manifest.json",
  "publication_derivation: task-f01.qmd#f01-01-derive-components",
  "forest_floor_loads: pre-PCT only",
  "forest_floor_method: Finney-Martin 1993 model 3 cumulative-load partition",
  paste0(
    "litter-load-boundary-cases: ",
    sum(forest_floor_pre_station$litter_load_bounded_at_zero)
  ),
  "post-PCT-forest-floor-loads: deliberately omitted pending protocol validity",
  "PCT-primary-contrast: pre-PCT minus post-PCT woody standing vegetation"
)
provenance_connection <- file(file.path(paths$manifests, "input-provenance.yml"), open = "wb")
writeLines(provenance_lines, provenance_connection, sep = "\n", useBytes = TRUE)
close(provenance_connection)
})

local({
publication_root <- .publication_render$root
script_dir <- file.path(publication_root, "scripts", "fuel")
paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

library(dplyr)
library(readr)

paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
components <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-components-transect.rds"))
paired <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-paired-transect.rds"))

add_design_groups <- function(data) {
  data |>
    mutate(
      block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
      design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE)
    )
}

component_data <- components |>
  mutate(component = as.character(component)) |>
  add_design_groups()

component_summary <- component_data |>
  summarise(
    n_transects = n(),
    n_sites = n_distinct(site),
    n_blocks = n_distinct(block),
    n_corners = n_distinct(design_corner),
    n_zero = sum(load_mgha == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_zero = mean(load_mgha == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(load_mgha)),
    mean_mgha = mean(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_mgha = sd(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance_mgha = var(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv = if_else(mean_mgha > 0, sd_mgha / mean_mgha, NA_real_),
    min_mgha = min(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25_mgha = quantile(load_mgha, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
    median_mgha = median(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75_mgha = quantile(load_mgha, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
    max_mgha = max(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c("phase", "component", "treatment")
  ) |>
  arrange(phase, component, treatment)

component_candidates <- component_data |>
  summarise(
    n_zero = sum(load_mgha == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_transects = n(),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(load_mgha)),
    .by = c("phase", "component")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    response_type = "nonnegative continuous load",
    fixed_effects = "treatment",
    random_effects = "(1 | site) + (1 | site:treatment) + (1 | site:treatment:corner)",
    conditional_family = if_else(n_zero > 0, "ziGamma(link = log)", "Gamma(link = log)"),
    zero_inflation_candidates = if_else(
      n_zero > 0,
      "~1; consider ~treatment only if zero-process diagnostics and replication support it",
      "none unless later diagnostics identify a structural-zero process"
    ),
    dispersion_candidates = "~1 first; compare ~treatment only if residual dispersion diagnostics support it",
    status = if_else(
      n_missing > 0,
      "candidate specifications only; resolve missing values before model fitting",
      "candidate specifications only; no model fitted"
    )

  arrange(phase, component)

  status = "candidate specification only; no model fitted"
)

title: F01 — fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
03 — Fit phase-component candidates
Purpose. Fit every predeclared phase-component candidate and retain its diagnostics.
Rationale. Use Gamma/log for positive loads and zero-inflated Gamma/log where zeros occur, retaining the existing zero-count threshold and post-PCT 100-hour sensitivities. Preserve all attempted fits and warnings. DHARMa uses 1,000 unconditional simulations with seed 20260918.


Calculation — f01-03-fit-phase-components


task_progress("f01-03-fit-phase-components")
local({
# Preserve the fresh-Rscript RNG boundary of this historical fitting stage.
# DHARMa 0.5.0 consumes an extra draw when .Random.seed is initially absent.
if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE))
  rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
publication_root <- .publication_render$root
script_dir <- file.path(publication_root, "scripts", "fuel")
paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

source(file.path(script_dir, "03-model-utils.R"))

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)

paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
output_paths <- model_output_paths(paths)
# This stage owns all pre/post phase-component artifacts. Clear only its prior
# artifacts so an idempotent rerun cannot retain a candidate no longer tested.
for (directory in c(output_paths$models, output_paths$diagnostics)) {
  stale <- list.files(directory, pattern = "^(pre|post)pct_", full.names = TRUE)
  if (length(stale)) file.remove(stale)
}
components <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-components-transect.rds")) |>
  mutate(
    component = as.character(component),
    block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
    design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE)
  )

design_formula <- load_mgha ~ treatment +
  (1 | site) + (1 | block) + (1 | design_corner)

fit_component_candidates <- function(data, phase_value, component_value) {
  model_data <- data |>
    filter(
      .data$phase == .env$phase_value,
      .data$component == .env$component_value,
      !is.na(load_mgha)
    )
  zero_count <- sum(model_data$load_mgha == 0)
  prefix <- paste(phase_value, component_value, sep = "_")

  candidates <- list()
  if (zero_count > 0) {
    candidates[["base"]] <- list(glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)", ~1, "~1", ~1, "~1")
    candidates[["disp_treatment"]] <- list(glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)", ~1, "~1", ~treatment, "~treatment")
    if (zero_count >= 8) {
      candidates[["zi_treatment"]] <- list(glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)", ~treatment, "~treatment", ~1, "~1")
    }
  } else {
    candidates[["base"]] <- list(Gamma(link = "log"), "Gamma(link = log)", ~0, "~0", ~1, "~1")
    candidates[["disp_treatment"]] <- list(Gamma(link = "log"), "Gamma(link = log)", ~0, "~0", ~treatment, "~treatment")
  }

  # The thesis used site plus treatment in both the zero and dispersion
  # submodels for post-PCT 100-hour fuels. Retain that candidate and add one
  # deliberately more complex site-by-treatment dispersion sensitivity check.
  if (phase_value == "postpct" && component_value == "hundhr") {
    candidates[["zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site"]] <- list(
      glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ~treatment + site, "~treatment + site",
      ~treatment + site, "~treatment + site"
    )
    candidates[["zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site_interaction"]] <- list(
      glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"), "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ~treatment + site, "~treatment + site",
      ~treatment * site, "~treatment * site"
    )
  }

  imap_dfr(candidates, function(candidate, candidate_name) {
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000, simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = paste(prefix, candidate_name, sep = "_"),
      response = component_value,
      analysis = paste(phase_value, "phase-specific component", sep = ": "),
      data = model_data,
      formula = design_formula,
      family = candidate[[1]],
      family_label = candidate[[2]],
      ziformula = candidate[[3]],
      ziformula_label = candidate[[4]],
      dispformula = candidate[[5]],
      dispformula_label = candidate[[6]],
      paths = paths
    )
  })
}

registry <- components |>
  distinct(phase, component) |>
  arrange(phase, component) |>
  pmap_dfr(function(phase, component) {
    fit_component_candidates(components, phase, component)
  })

write_csv(registry, file.path(paths$manifests, "phase-component-model-registry.csv"))
})

Purpose. Represent both joint woody phase loads and signed matched reduction.
Rationale. The joint model retains transect pairing. Signed reduction also has Gaussian and Student-t candidates; it is not automatically a Gamma response. Keep the existing zero/dispersion candidate sets and diagnostic protocol.

task_progress("f01-04-fit-woody-pct-models")
local({
# This stage formerly started in a separate Rscript process. Restore its empty
# initial RNG state; the diagnostic seed and unconditional simulations are unchanged.
if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE))
  rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
publication_root <- .publication_render$root
script_dir <- file.path(publication_root, "scripts", "fuel")
paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

source(file.path(script_dir, "03-model-utils.R"))

library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)

paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
output_paths <- model_output_paths(paths)
# This stage owns all repeated-woody and paired-contrast artifacts.
for (directory in c(output_paths$models, output_paths$diagnostics)) {
  stale <- list.files(directory, pattern = "^woody_", full.names = TRUE)
  if (length(stale)) file.remove(stale)
}
paired <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-paired-transect.rds")) |>
  mutate(
    block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
    design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE),
    transect_id = interaction(site, treatment, corner, azi, drop = TRUE)
  )

woody_long <- paired |>
  select(site, treatment, corner, azi, block, design_corner, transect_id, woody_vegetation_prepct, woody_vegetation_postpct) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("woody_vegetation_"),
    names_to = "phase",
    names_prefix = "woody_vegetation_",
    values_to = "load_mgha"
  ) |>
  mutate(phase = factor(phase, levels = c("prepct", "postpct")))

Calculation — f01-05-evaluate-and-select-models


task_progress("f01-05-evaluate-and-select-models")
local({
publication_root <- .publication_render$root
script_dir <- file.path(publication_root, "scripts", "fuel")
paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

library(dplyr)
library(readr)

paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
registry_files <- c(
  file.path(paths$manifests, "phase-component-model-registry.csv"),
  file.path(paths$manifests, "woody-pct-model-registry.csv")
)
if (!all(file.exists(registry_files))) {
  stop("F01 candidate fits are missing; recompute this task from the beginning. See publication/README.md.")
}

registry <- bind_rows(lapply(registry_files, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)) |>
  mutate(
    comparison_group = paste(response, analysis, sep = " | ")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    aic_rank = if_else(fit_status == "fit", rank(aic, ties.method = "min"), NA_real_),
    delta_aic = if_else(
      fit_status == "fit",
      aic - min(aic[fit_status == "fit"], na.rm = TRUE),
      NA_real_
    ),
    .by = comparison_group
  ) |>

Objective
Produce a compact, reviewable full-inventory figure (and caption) from the current AIC-leading fitted publication models. Use nine panels: paired pre-/ post-PCT estimates for 1-, 10-, 100-, and 1,000-hour fuels plus woody and herbaceous vegetation; pre-PCT-only panels for litter and duff; and a separate matched woody-vegetation-difference panel (pre-PCT minus post-PCT). Constraints and starting material
The upstream F01 record supplies component definitions, saved fitted-model candidates, diagnostics, and provisional leaders. RD04 consumes these artifacts; changes to their derivation or fitting belong in F01.

Use the saved fitted models identified as AIC leaders in the F01 model-selection register. Their diagnostic/scientific review remains visible through the figure-review decision rather than blocking draft generation.
Integrate over all fitted random effects for a consistent mean-load interpretation, with equal study-site weights. Derive woody mean change from the same joint phase model as the woody load panels, retaining its pre/post covariance.
Retain the thesis visual grammar—model estimate point with a colored 95% CI range—for the six paired panels. Label pre-PCT-only litter and duff panels explicitly; do not imply a post-PCT zero or estimate.
Plot the matched woody vegetation difference separately with a zero reference line. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load, so it must not be styled as another phase estimate.
Use panel-specific y-scales and a 3 × 3 layout to keep the broad load range legible. Keep full model registries, diagnostics, and pairwise comparisons in linked artifacts rather than adding them to the figure.

text:
07 — Audit prediction and uncertainty
Purpose. Verify the response means and their uncertainty against independent computational routes and exported thesis references.
Rationale. Integrate over all fitted random intercepts, include modeled zeros, and give each study-site context equal weight. Carry the full parameter covariance through the gradient, including random-effect variances and joint woody pre/post covariance. F01 supplies saved models; this audit does not refit or select them.


Calculation — rd04-07-audit-rd04-inference


task_begin("RD04")
source("scripts/fuel/00-fuel-config.R")
task_progress("rd04-07-audit-rd04-inference")
local({
publication_root <- .publication_render$root
script_dir <- file.path(publication_root, "scripts", "fuel")
paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(glmmTMB)
  library(marginaleffects)
  library(readr)
  library(tidyr)
})
models_dir <- file.path(task_root("F01"), "fuel", "models")
audit_dir <- file.path(paths_common$output, "fuel/inference-audit")
dir.create(audit_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Evaluate only these two definitions, never the original script's output steps.
original_script <- file.path(script_dir, "retired", "06-generate-rd04-figure.R")
original_hash <- tools::md5sum(original_script)
for (expr in parse(original_script)) {
  if (is.call(expr) && identical(expr[[1]], as.name("<-")) && is.symbol(expr[[2]]) &&
      as.character(expr[[2]]) %in% c("model_ids", "model_estimates")) eval(expr)
}

source(file.path(script_dir, "rd04-inference-utils.R"))

spec <- tibble(
  key = names(model_ids), model_id = unname(model_ids),
  component = c("1-hour", "1-hour", "10-hour", "10-hour", "100-hour", "100-hour",
                "1,000-hour", "1,000-hour", "Woody vegetation", "Herbaceous vegetation",
                "Herbaceous vegetation", "Litter", "Duff", "Woody difference"),
  phase = c(rep(c("prepct", "postpct"), 4), NA, "prepct", "postpct", "prepct", "prepct", NA)
)
spec <- bind_rows(filter(spec, key != "woody_phase"),
                  mutate(filter(spec, key == "woody_phase"), phase = "prepct"),
                  mutate(filter(spec, key == "woody_phase"), phase = "postpct"))

audit <- list()
structures <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(spec))) {
  item <- spec[i, ]
  message("Auditing ", item$model_id, " ", item$phase)
  model <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, paste0(item$model_id, ".rds")))
  phase_arg <- if (is.na(item$phase)) NULL else item$phase
  grid <- reference_grid(model, phase_arg)
  avg <- averaging_matrix(grid)
  reference <- custom_reference(model, grid)
  me <- as.data.frame(avg_predictions(model, newdata = grid, type = "response",
                       by = intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid)),
                       re.form = NA, allow.new.levels = TRUE))
  me <- me[match(as.character(reference$treatment), as.character(me$treatment)), ]
  legacy <- model_estimates(item$model_id, item$component, phase_arg,
                            difference = item$key == "woody_difference")
  legacy <- legacy[match(as.character(reference$treatment), as.character(legacy$treatment)), ]
  s <- integration_setup(model, grid)
  integrated <- custom_integrated(s)
  me_integrated <- as.data.frame(marginaleffects_integrated(s))
  stopifnot(max(abs(reference$estimate - me$estimate)) < 1e-6,
            max(abs(reference$std.error - me$std.error) / pmax(1, reference$std.error)) < 1e-4,
            max(abs(reference$estimate - legacy$estimate)) < 1e-6,
            max(abs(integrated$estimate - me_integrated$estimate)) < 1e-6,
            max(abs(integrated$se - me_integrated$std.error) / pmax(1, integrated$se)) < 1e-4)
  # Verify integration at a point using numerical quadrature, independently of
  # the closed-form exp(v/2) calculation (including near-zero variances).
  if (s$link == "log") {
    quadrature <- integrate(function(z) exp(sqrt(s$variance) * z) * dnorm(z),
                            lower = -12, upper = 12, rel.tol = 1e-9)$value
    stopifnot(abs(quadrature - exp(s$variance / 2)) < 1e-7)
  }
  # Check matrix construction against the model's own predict implementation.
  row0 <- if (s$link == "log") exp(drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])) else drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])
  if (length(s$iz)) row0 <- row0 * (1 - plogis(drop(s$Z %*% s$par[s$iz])))
  stopifnot(max(abs(row0 - predict(model, grid, type = "response", re.form = NA))) < 1e-6)
  # Average ALL observed rows within site, then equally across sites; retaining
  # only one corner/transect per site would give an arbitrary conditional mean.
  observed <- model$frame
  if (!is.null(phase_arg) && "phase" %in% names(observed)) observed <- filter(observed, .data$phase == .env$phase_arg)
  conditional <- observed |>
    mutate(predicted = as.numeric(predict(model, observed, type = "response", re.form = NULL))) |>
    group_by(across(all_of(intersect(c("site", "treatment", "phase"), names(observed))))) |>
    summarise(predicted = mean(predicted), .groups = "drop") |>
    group_by(across(all_of(intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(observed))))) |>
    summarise(predicted = mean(predicted), .groups = "drop")
  fitted_groups <- conditional$predicted[match(as.character(reference$treatment), as.character(conditional$treatment))]
  # Marginal mean intervals: log-delta intervals stay positive without truncation;
  # the signed identity-link difference uses ordinary response-scale intervals.
  lcl <- if (s$link == "log") integrated$estimate * exp(-qnorm(.975) * integrated$se / integrated$estimate) else integrated$estimate - qnorm(.975) * integrated$se
  ucl <- if (s$link == "log") integrated$estimate * exp(qnorm(.975) * integrated$se / integrated$estimate) else integrated$estimate + qnorm(.975) * integrated$se
  audit[[i]] <- tibble(
    model_id = item$model_id, component = item$component, phase = item$phase,
    treatment = as.character(reference$treatment), n_sites = rowSums(avg$A > 0),
    reference_custom = reference$estimate, reference_marginaleffects = me$estimate,
    original_se = legacy$se, corrected_reference_se = reference$std.error,
    marginaleffects_reference_se = me$std.error,
    fitted_group_site_balanced_mean = fitted_groups,
    random_intercept_variance = s$variance,
    integration_multiplier = if (s$link == "log") exp(s$variance / 2) else 1,
    integrated_custom = integrated$estimate,
    integrated_marginaleffects = me_integrated$estimate,
    integrated_se_custom = integrated$se,
    integrated_se_marginaleffects = me_integrated$std.error,
    integrated_lcl = lcl, integrated_ucl = ucl
  )
  structures[[i]] <- tibble(model_id = item$model_id, phase = item$phase,
                            conditional = deparse1(formula(model)),
                            zero = deparse1(formula(model, component = "zi")),
                            dispersion = deparse1(formula(model, component = "disp")))
}
audit <- bind_rows(audit)
write_csv(audit, file.path(audit_dir, "rd04-estimand-comparison.csv"))
structure_path <- file.path(audit_dir, "model-structures.csv")
structure_table <- as.data.frame(bind_rows(structures))
# Preserve an unchanged model inventory, including when it is open for review.
if (!file.exists(structure_path) ||
    !identical(structure_table, as.data.frame(read_csv(structure_path, show_col_types = FALSE)))) {
  write_csv(structure_table, structure_path)
}

# A coherent mean change uses the same repeated-phase model on both sides and
# its cross-phase covariance. Compare with the independently fitted t model.
woody <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, paste0(model_ids[["woody_phase"]], ".rds")))
s <- integration_setup(woody, reference_grid(woody))
s <- woody_change_setup(s)
treatments <- as.character(s$avg$labels$treatment)
change <- custom_integrated(s)

title: RD04 — fuel phase and PCT display
text:
Prediction and interpretation review
Implemented approach: use study-standardized, population-averaged expected loads as the baseline for mean fuel loading in comparable systems. Integrate over the fitted random-intercept distributions and include modeled zeros, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts. Retain the historical zero-random-effect predictions as a clearly labeled reference/sensitivity summary in the audit. RD04 now uses this integrated interpretation throughout, with woody mean change derived from the joint phase model; the fitted load models remain provisional pending scientific review. The original generator has been retired in favor of the stage-08 calculation on this page.

What the prediction arguments actually do








Calculation
Quantity estimated
Appropriate interpretation




re.form = NULL with known grouping IDs
Expected response conditional on fitted random effects for those sites, blocks, corners, and transects
Conditions in the sampled units; average over an explicitly weighted set of these units if that is the target


re.form = NA (or ~0)
Expected response with all random effects set to zero
A reference at the center of the latent random-effect distribution


re.form = NULL, with selected random-only grouping variables set to NA in newdata
Retains known-group effects for the remaining grouping variables and sets the selected groups’ effects to zero
A conditional reference, e.g., a known site with zero lower-level effects


Integrate expected responses over the fitted random-effect distribution
Arithmetic expected load for a population of exchangeable sampling units
The model-based mean-load baseline used in RD04



marginaleffects passes the random-effect arguments to the fitted model’s prediction method. Its by argument and avg_predictions() average the predictions supplied to them; they do not change zero-effect predictions into random-effect-integrated predictions. This distinction follows the mixed-model vignette, the prediction reference, and the distinction between observed-group averaging and new-group integration in the Bayesian vignette.
For glmmTMB, arbitrary formulas selecting random effects in re.form are not supported. Selected grouping variables can instead be set to NA, but this is unsuitable when a variable is also required as a fixed predictor: site, for example, must remain defined for the post-PCT 100-hour model’s zero component. allow.new.levels = TRUE permits new grouping IDs; it does not request integration over their possible effects. See the model’s prediction documentation.
Two different uses of “conditional” also need separating: type = "conditional" requests the conditional-distribution mean, whereas re.form controls conditioning on random effects. For these zero-inflated Gamma models, type = "response" returns \((1-p_0)\mu_+\), including the modeled probability of zero, while type = "conditional" returns \(\mu_+\). Dispersion parameters affect variability and estimation but are not additional multipliers of this response mean. Gamma sampling variability should not receive a lognormal residual-variance correction.


Alignment of the thesis code and interpretation
The controlling Results function is marginaleffects_to_emmeans() in analysis/thesis/results.qmd: both predictions and comparisons use re.form = NA. For fuel loads, its pre- and post-PCT calls use tidyr::expand(data, treatment, site), giving equal site weights. Passing the predictions and pairwise-difference standard errors into emmeans::emmobj() changes their representation, not their underlying estimand. The earlier re.form = NULL exploratory basal-area plots in regen_visualize.qmd are not the calls controlling the thesis Results.







Thesis statement or presentation
Assessment




Methods: predictions incorporate all components and average over random effects to obtain population means
Partly aligned: response predictions can include the zero component, but the wrapper sets random effects to zero before averaging. The random effects were not integrated out.


Methods: estimates apply to equal proportions of similar sites, specifically north- and south-facing aspects
Equal site weights are explicit for fuel grids. Zeroing site random effects does not reproduce an aspect mixture on a nonlinear response scale; aspect was not a fixed adjustment variable. Transport requires an exchangeability assumption beyond the prediction settings.


Fuel Results: “expected value” and “estimated marginal means”
Valid if identified as site-standardized expectations at zero random effects. Too broad if read as arithmetic population-average loads across forest heterogeneity.


Discussion: compare “average” loads with other forest studies
State whether each value is an observed mean, a zero-effect reference, or an integrated model mean, and check component definitions and sampling protocols. These quantities are not interchangeable.


Post-PCT caption: vegetation difference “represents slash fuels recruited to the forest floor”
Overstates the measurement: standing-vegetation reduction is an inferred potential contribution, not measured slash deposition. RD04’s qualified caption is better aligned.


Results: pre/post estimates are not statistically comparable because model structures differ
Different structures alone do not prevent comparison. Formal phase differences need an explicit common estimand and their covariance, accounting for pairing. Separate phase CIs do not supply a paired change test.


Discussion/conclusions: PCT “resulted in” or “generated” the observed dead-fuel changes
The observed transition supports association; attributing all change to PCT requires the design/time assumptions. No unthinned contemporaneous comparison is used by these predictions.



The same wrapper controls regeneration and sprout Results. Basal area, Douglas-fir counts, and year-10 height use nonlinear links, so zero-effect and integrated means can differ there too. Height increment uses an identity link; integration over mean-zero random effects leaves its expected value unchanged, for a fixed covariate distribution. The Results grids also vary: treatment height-increment summaries explicitly balance years, whereas the by-year analysis uses newdata = NULL and averages within observed species/year cells. Those are different standardization choices and should be described separately. The fuel integration code below is deliberately restricted to its audited model structures; it is not a general-purpose replacement for those other analyses.
One numerical provenance issue also deserves attention: the Discussion reports about 42 Mg/ha of pre-PCT 1,000-hour fuel. Reproducing the Results wrapper on the saved thesis models gives an equal-treatment reference mean of 32.63 Mg/ha. The Discussion value may be an observed summary, but it should not be presented as the grand mean of these particular model predictions without a separate source. The audit preserves all reproduced thesis fuel estimates.


How RD04 compares with the thesis
The original RD04 and thesis fuel Results used the same zero-random-effect target and equal-site weighting. Both used valid prediction grids: the thesis expanded the observed treatment and site levels, and RD04 retained observed rows with valid nested identifiers, one per site/treatment/phase. Neither approach introduced a grid discrepancy for these zero-effect predictions. The updated RD04 retains equal-site weighting and integrates over random effects. Every phase-specific mean averages four site contexts; post-PCT 100-hour fuel additionally retains fixed site effects in its zero component.
Numerical changes from the thesis to the original RD04 arose from revised fitted models and component definitions, not a switch from marginaleffects to custom prediction. Implemented target and worked demonstration
For a treatment \(t\), phase \(h\), and equally weighted site contexts \(s\), define
\[
M_{th} = \frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}
  E_b\!\left[(1-p_{0,sth})\exp\{x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta + z^{\mathsf T}b\}\right].
\]
The audited load models have independent Gaussian random intercepts only in the conditional model and no random effects in the zero component. Thus, with \(v=\sum_k\sigma_k^2\) across all modeled random-intercept levels,
\[
M_{th}=\exp(v/2)\,
\frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}(1-p_{0,sth})\exp(x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta).
\]
This is exact under the fitted model, not a generic bias-correction option. The same multiplier across treatments within a fitted load model preserves ratios and rankings, while changing absolute loads and differences. Inference must still propagate uncertainty in the multiplier; old p-values and standard errors should not simply be carried over.
The separate Student-t difference model was replaced in the display by the integrated joint phase-model contrast so that woody change equals the difference between the displayed arithmetic mean loads. Its uncertainty retains the joint pre/post covariance, keeping the change estimate consistent with the matched design and the mean-load interpretation of the other panels.
For post-PCT 100-hour fuel, “site-standardized” specifically retains an equal mixture of the four fitted zero-process site contexts. Integration of the random intercepts cannot create a zero-process coefficient for a fifth site. The baseline therefore concerns comparable contexts, not a fitted prediction for any arbitrary new forest. Four sites also provide limited information about the site-variance distribution. A regional mean, or an explicitly 50:50 aspect-standardized mean, would need a justified target distribution and sufficient covariate information to support that standardization.
The demonstration holds fitted load models fixed and changes the estimand; woody change now uses their joint phase model. Selected GS examples below show why the distinction matters (Mg/ha). The intervals describe uncertainty in the integrated mean, not variation in a new forest or transect.

The implementation in the executable audit above demonstrates both routes:

Historical reference target: marginaleffects::avg_predictions(model, newdata = grid, by = ..., type = "response", re.form = NA) agrees with predict() followed by explicit matrix averaging. The custom variance is A %*% prediction$cov.fit %*% t(A).
Implemented integrated target: a nonlinear functional supplied to marginaleffects::hypotheses() averages the response means after analytic integration. A separate custom implementation derives its gradient and calculates G %*% V %*% t(G). Both use the full covariance of the fitted nonrandom parameters, including zero-model coefficients, log random-effect standard deviations, and their cross-covariances. Merely multiplying an avg_predictions() interval by exp(v/2) would omit uncertainty in \(v\).

The hypotheses documentation supports nonlinear functionals and supplied covariance matrices. Here the full parameter table is supplied explicitly because ordinary fixed-coefficient prediction covariance alone does not include the integration multiplier’s variance. These are asymptotic delta-method intervals, conditional on the chosen models and the reference grid. They do not include model-selection or fuel-component-derivation uncertainty. Refitted parametric bootstrap intervals are a useful final sensitivity check, particularly for herbaceous loads with large variance corrections and only four sites.
Verification: the audit checks all 60 historical comparison cells for agreement of reference point estimates and SEs, integrated point estimates, and integrated SEs; the latter agree within a relative/absolute tolerance of \(10^{-4}\). It checks the integration multiplier against numerical quadrature, the matrix predictions against predict.glmmTMB(), and the retired script’s checksum before and after the run. It additionally verifies all four woody mean contrasts with cross-phase covariance and reproduces the 48 thesis fuel reference estimates. Outputs and the R/package session record are in publication/outputs/fuel/inference-audit/.
Review the complete audit and inference-helper source.


Methods wording
For the implemented population-average baseline:

We estimated treatment- and phase-specific mean fuel loads by averaging response-scale expectations, including modeled zeros, over an equally weighted grid of the four study-site contexts and analytically integrating over all fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances.

The matched-contrast qualification can be stated in its own Methods sentence:

Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

summarize_integrated <- function(s, component, model_id, phase = NULL, difference = FALSE) {
  prediction <- custom_integrated(s)
  # Means use log-delta intervals; signed differences use response-scale ones.
  low <- if (difference) prediction$estimate - qnorm(.975) * prediction$se else
    prediction$estimate * exp(-qnorm(.975) * prediction$se / prediction$estimate)
  high <- if (difference) prediction$estimate + qnorm(.975) * prediction$se else
    prediction$estimate * exp(qnorm(.975) * prediction$se / prediction$estimate)
  labels <- s$avg$labels
  phase_values <- if (difference) rep("Vegetation difference", nrow(labels)) else {
    values <- if ("phase" %in% names(labels)) as.character(labels$phase) else rep(phase, nrow(labels))
    stopifnot(all(values %in% c("prepct", "postpct")))
    ifelse(values == "prepct", "Pre-PCT", "Post-PCT")
  }
  tibble(component = component, phase = phase_values,
         treatment = as.character(labels$treatment), estimate = prediction$estimate,
         se = prediction$se, lcl = low, ucl = high, model_id = model_id,
         estimand = if (difference) "integrated matched woody mean difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)" else
           "site-standardized random-effect-integrated expected load",
         interval_method = if (difference) "response-scale delta method with joint phase covariance" else
           "log-scale delta method for integrated mean",
         random_intercept_variance = s$variance)
}

Publication execution
RD04 inference, audits and display generation use the sole publication environment: R 4.6.2 with publication/renv.lock. Historical thesis reference calculations belong to the separate thesis export operation. Publication consumes those exported reference values; it has no previous-environment replay or retained migration acceptance/difference artifacts.








Figure 1: RD04 full fuel inventory by retention treatment. Points are site-standardized mean loads from AIC-leading models, integrated over all fitted random effects and including modeled zeros; ranges are 95% confidence intervals for the means. Study sites receive equal weights. Orange denotes pre-PCT and blue denotes post-PCT for the six components measured in both phases. Litter and duff are pre-PCT only. The woody vegetation-difference panel is the pre-PCT minus post-PCT mean contrast from the joint matched woody phase model, with its pre/post covariance. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load. Panel-specific y-scales are used.

# Keep valid nested identifiers from one observed row per site/treatment/phase.
# These identifiers do not contribute fitted random effects when re.form=NA.
write_publication_lines <- function(text, path) {
  connection <- file(path, open = "wb")
  on.exit(close(connection))
  writeLines(enc2utf8(sub("[[:blank:]]+$", "", text)), connection,
             sep = "\n", useBytes = TRUE)
}

reference_grid <- function(model, phase = NULL) {
  keys <- intersect(c("site", "treatment", "phase"), names(model$frame))
  grid <- distinct(model$frame, across(all_of(keys)), .keep_all = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(phase) && "phase" %in% keys) grid <- filter(grid, .data$phase == .env$phase)
  counts <- count(grid, treatment)
  stopifnot(length(unique(counts$n)) == 1L)
  grid
}

# A maps row predictions to equally weighted site means. A V A' retains every
# cross-site covariance; treating site predictions as independent is incorrect.
averaging_matrix <- function(grid) {
  keys <- intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid))
  labels <- distinct(grid, across(all_of(keys)))
  A <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(labels)), function(i) {
    keep <- Reduce(`&`, lapply(keys, function(k) grid[[k]] == labels[[k]][i]))
    as.numeric(keep) / sum(keep)
  }, numeric(nrow(grid))))
  list(A = A, labels = labels)
}

custom_reference <- function(model, grid) {
  p <- predict(model, newdata = grid, type = "response", re.form = NA,
               allow.new.levels = TRUE, se.fit = TRUE, cov.fit = TRUE)
  avg <- averaging_matrix(grid)
  transform(avg$labels, estimate = as.vector(avg$A %*% p$fit),
            std.error = sqrt(diag(avg$A %*% p$cov.fit %*% t(avg$A))))
}

# Exact integration for THESE models: independent Gaussian random intercepts in
# the conditional model, log/identity link, no random effects in the zero model.
# This deliberately fails on slopes, correlated effects, offsets, or other links.
integration_setup <- function(model, grid) {
  vc <- VarCorr(model)
  stopifnot(length(vc$zi) == 0L, length(vc$disp) == 0L,
            all(vapply(vc$cond, function(x) identical(dim(x), c(1L, 1L)), logical(1))))
  X <- model.matrix(delete.response(terms(formula(model, fixed.only = TRUE))), grid)
  Z <- model.matrix(formula(model, component = "zi", fixed.only = TRUE), grid)
  par <- model$fit$par
  ib <- which(names(par) == "beta")
  iz <- which(names(par) == "betazi")
  it <- which(names(par) == "theta")
  stopifnot(ncol(X) == length(ib), ncol(Z) == length(iz),
            length(it) == length(vc$cond), model$sdr$pdHess,
            isTRUE(all.equal(unname(par), unname(model$sdr$par.fixed))),
            is.null(model.offset(model$frame)),
            family(model)$link %in% c("log", "identity"))
  variance <- sum(vapply(vc$cond, function(x) x[1, 1], numeric(1)))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(variance, sum(exp(2 * par[it])), tolerance = 1e-8)))
  list(X = X, Z = Z, par = par, V = model$sdr$cov.fixed,
       ib = ib, iz = iz, it = it, link = family(model)$link,
       avg = averaging_matrix(grid), variance = variance)
}

# Independent analytic derivatives for the custom delta-method implementation.
custom_integrated <- function(s) {
  eta <- drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])
  pzero <- if (length(s$iz)) plogis(drop(s$Z %*% s$par[s$iz])) else rep(0, length(eta))
  if (s$link == "log") {
    mu <- exp(eta + s$variance / 2) * (1 - pzero)
    D <- matrix(0, nrow(s$X), length(s$par))
    D[, s$ib] <- mu * s$X
    if (length(s$iz)) D[, s$iz] <- -mu * pzero * s$Z
    D[, s$it] <- outer(mu, exp(2 * s$par[s$it]))
  } else {
    stopifnot(length(s$iz) == 0L)
    mu <- eta
    D <- matrix(0, nrow(s$X), length(s$par))
    D[, s$ib] <- s$X
  }
  G <- s$avg$A %*% D
  list(estimate = drop(s$avg$A %*% mu),
       se = sqrt(pmax(0, diag(G %*% s$V %*% t(G)))), G = G)
}

# Contrast the same matched model's integrated phase means, retaining their
# covariance through a single gradient and the full parameter covariance.
woody_change_setup <- function(s) {
  labels <- s$avg$labels
  stopifnot(all(c("phase", "treatment") %in% names(labels)),
            setequal(unique(as.character(labels$phase)), c("prepct", "postpct")))
  treatments <- unique(as.character(labels$treatment))
  C <- t(vapply(treatments, function(trt) {
    stopifnot(sum(labels$treatment == trt & labels$phase == "prepct") == 1L,
              sum(labels$treatment == trt & labels$phase == "postpct") == 1L)
    as.numeric(labels$treatment == trt) * ifelse(labels$phase == "prepct", 1, -1)
  }, numeric(nrow(labels))))
  s$avg$A <- C %*% s$avg$A
  s$avg$labels <- data.frame(treatment = treatments)
  s
}

# marginaleffects does the nonlinear delta method on a supplied full parameter
# table, including theta (log SDs), not just the conditional fixed coefficients.
# avg_predictions(re.form=NA) alone does NOT integrate over random effects.
marginaleffects_integrated <- function(s) {
  parameters <- data.frame(term = paste0("p", seq_along(s$par)),
                           estimate = unname(s$par))
  functional <- function(x) {
    b <- x$estimate
    eta <- drop(s$X %*% b[s$ib])
    pzero <- if (length(s$iz)) plogis(drop(s$Z %*% b[s$iz])) else rep(0, length(eta))
    mu <- if (s$link == "log") exp(eta + sum(exp(2 * b[s$it])) / 2) * (1 - pzero) else eta
    data.frame(term = seq_len(nrow(s$avg$labels)), estimate = drop(s$avg$A %*% mu))
  }
  marginaleffects::hypotheses(parameters, hypothesis = functional, vcov = s$V,
             numderiv = "fdcenter", conf_level = .95)
}

# Predict at every observed site-by-treatment (and phase, where relevant)
# combination, excluding random effects. Average the balanced site predictions
# within each plotted treatment/phase and propagate their prediction covariance
# to retain model-based uncertainty for the displayed marginal estimate.
model_estimates <- function(model_id, component, phase = NULL, difference = FALSE) {
  model <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, paste0(model_id, ".rds")))
  phase_label <- if (difference) {
    "Vegetation difference"
  } else if (identical(phase, "prepct")) {
    "Pre-PCT"
  } else {
    "Post-PCT"
  }
  frame <- model$frame
  focal <- c("treatment", if ("phase" %in% names(frame)) "phase")
  grid_columns <- intersect(c("site", focal), names(frame))
  grid <- frame |>
    distinct(across(all_of(grid_columns)), .keep_all = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(phase) && "phase" %in% names(grid)) {
    grid <- filter(grid, .data$phase == .env$phase)
  }
  prediction <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = grid,
    type = "response",
    se.fit = TRUE,
    cov.fit = TRUE,
    re.form = NA,
    allow.new.levels = TRUE
  )
  grid <- mutate(grid, estimate_site = as.numeric(prediction$fit))
  group_columns <- intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid))
  groups <- grid |>
    mutate(row_id = row_number()) |>
    group_by(across(all_of(group_columns))) |>
    summarise(row_ids = list(row_id), estimate = mean(estimate_site), .groups = "drop")
  groups <- groups |>
    rowwise() |>
    mutate(
      se = sqrt(sum(prediction$cov.fit[row_ids[[1]], row_ids[[1]], drop = FALSE]) / length(row_ids[[1]])^2),
      lcl = estimate - stats::qnorm(0.975) * se,
      ucl = estimate + stats::qnorm(0.975) * se
    ) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(
      component = component,
      model_id = model_id,
      estimand = if (difference) "matched woody vegetation difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)" else "phase-specific expected load",
      phase = phase_label,
      lcl = if (difference) lcl else pmax(0, lcl),
      treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c("gs", "ld", "ha", "hd"))
    )
  select(groups, component, phase, treatment, estimate, se, lcl, ucl, model_id, estimand)
}

title: Development workflow
text: This overview describes the publication-development process. The task register and task list summarize the work, and each task has a dedicated review page. Each task is tracked like a small issue: it begins with an objective and guardrails, records the decisions and artifacts produced while it is open, and ends either in a reviewable manuscript product or a completed analytical record. The manuscript is developed backwards from the results displays: figures and tables → results → methods → discussion → introduction → abstract → title. This order adapts the “write backwards” approach described by Montagnes, Montagnes, and Yang (2022).

title: Development workflow
text:
How to use this queue
Each dedicated task page preserves its proposal and detailed review record. Review and edit that proposal, then move the task through this sequence:
Direction for review → Approved to execute → In progress → Pending review → Accepted (or Revision requested) → Complete.
“Queued” means the task is deliberately decomposed and ready to be proposed; it is not yet authorized for execution. “Completed — analytical record” means the reproducible work is preserved, while a decision explicitly marked provisional still awaits scientific review. Page targets are working allocations for the main manuscript, not a journal requirement.

Documentation responsibilities
The analytical sequence starts with F01, followed by RD04 and RT03 Results writing. Each step’s executable QMD owns the detailed record: purpose/scope, inputs/dependencies, analyses performed, outputs/findings, decisions/rationale, implications/handoff, and review state/history. Update the originating step when its analysis or decision changes; downstream steps link to that record and explain their own use of it.
F01 owns fuel derivation, exploration, candidate fitting, and provisional model leaders. RD04 owns prediction/inference, uncertainty, the figure/estimates, and retired display history. RT03 owns the Results claims and qualifications. M03 and D03 will own manuscript Methods wording and management interpretation when their queued work begins. Consuming an upstream artifact does not transfer its ownership or accept its provisional scientific decisions.
For the developed fuel records, tasks.json separates produced outputs from consumed inputs and lists depends_on task IDs. Task introductions and file lists provide navigation; analytical explanations remain on their owning pages. Task summaries are concise descriptions of those records, not another decision log. The publication guide supplies operational commands and links back to the step documentation.
Calculation specifications and order live directly in each owning task page. Quarto selects whole pages for recomputation through native execution parameters; unselected pages review saved artifacts. There is no pipeline map, combined analytical account, or document-execution loop. See the maintenance guide for modes and validation.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Forest managers using retention forestry need information on regeneration and fuel development to design productive stands in fire-adapted ecosystems. We analyzed 10-year remeasurement data from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment in Jackson Demonstration State Forest, California. The experiment compared group selection, aggregated retention, and low- and high-density dispersed retention treatments and measured regeneration, sprout growth, and surface fuel loading.
Redwood regeneration responded strongly to increasing canopy openness, whereas tanoak responses were more modest. Sprout-height findings will remain part of the main regeneration evidence. Fuel measurements describe conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including the PCT-associated contrast. The manuscript will evaluate how overstory retention affects regeneration while presenting fuel components in a form useful for integrated silviculture, fuels, and fire management.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Study area and design
The experiment is located in the Jackson Demonstration State Forest in coastal northern California. Four harvest treatments were replicated at four sites in 2012: group selection (GS), high-density dispersed retention (HD), high-density aggregated retention (HA), and low-density dispersed retention (LD). The retained-overstory treatments targeted post-harvest relative densities of 13% or 21%; group selection created a 1-ha opening with a lightly thinned buffer. These treatments were designed to examine alternative pathways for developing multiaged redwood stands (Berrill & O’Hara, 2009; Reineke, 1933).
Ten years after harvest, regeneration plots and fuel transects were established within each 0.2-ha treatment macro plot. Regeneration measurements characterized redwood, tanoak, and Douglas-fir; fuel transects characterized dead surface fuels and live vegetation. The plots were remeasured after precommercial thinning, which released selected conifers from competing trees and shrubs.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Analysis
Detailed sampling procedures, model diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses will be retained as supplementary material.

Regeneration basal area
Basal area was modeled separately for redwood, tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species using zero-inflated Gamma mixed models with a conditional log link. Treatment was a fixed effect; site and macro plot nested within site were random intercepts. Each species category had its own intercept-only zero and dispersion components. Each model used 64 vegetation-plot observations from four sites and 16 macro plots. Arithmetic mean basal area included modeled zeros and integrated over both fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. Confidence intervals for the means were calculated using the log-scale delta method with the full parameter covariance, including random-effect variance uncertainty. Redwood and tanoak estimates are displayed in the Results; estimates for all four categories are reported in the supplement.


Fuel loads and PCT contrast
Reported values are model-based arithmetic mean loads, including modeled zeros and integrating over fitted random effects, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts.
These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. section: Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning
text:
Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning

Dead fuel loading
Fuel measurements ten years after harvest characterized conditions before and after precommercial thinning (PCT) across the four retention treatments (Figure 2). Following PCT, group selection (GS) and low-density dispersed retention (LD) showed the largest estimated increases in fine dead-fuel loads and reductions in woody standing vegetation. These treatments also had the highest post-PCT fine dead-fuel loads. Pre-PCT dead-fuel estimates suggested subtler, component-specific treatment patterns. Fuel loads are reported as model-estimated means, with 95% confidence intervals. Woody and herbaceous standing vegetation are reported separately, as are pre-PCT litter and duff. All loads and load differences below are in Mg ha-1.
Before PCT, estimated 1-hour fuel loads were highest in high-density aggregated retention (HA; 1.2) and lowest in GS (0.6), with LD and high-density dispersed (HD) retention intermediate. Estimated 10-hour loads ranged from 2.8 in HD to 3.8 in GS, and 100-hour loads from 9.0 to 11.5 in those same treatments. The 1,000-hour class had larger mean loads, ranging from 30.2 in LD to 49.6 (95% CI 25.9 to 95.0) in GS. Uncertainty was substantial for this coarse-wood component across treatments.
The separated forest-floor components showed different treatment patterns. Pre-PCT litter estimates ranged from 12.6 in LD to 18.4 in GS; HA and HD were intermediate. Duff estimates were lowest in HA, at 19.3 (95% CI 14.5 to 25.8), and highest in HD, at 35.5 (95% CI 26.6 to 47.4), with GS and LD both near 28–29. These are model-derived forest-floor loads based on the estimated litter-depth boundary. Post-PCT litter and duff were not estimated because the forest-floor boundary could not be distinguished reliably in the presence of slash and suspended foliage.
After PCT, estimated 1-hour loads were about 2.4–2.7 in GS, LD, and HD, and 1.4 in HA. The 10-hour estimates were ordered GS (9.6), LD (5.9), HA (4.1), and HD (3.3). Pre-PCT woody standing-vegetation means were greatest in GS (39.9), followed by LD (26.5), HD (18.8), and HA (14.7). Post-PCT means were 2.0–2.9 across treatments. All four reduction intervals excluded zero. Their uncertainty includes the pre/post covariance; the ordering of reduction estimates alone does not test differences among treatments.
Herbaceous standing-vegetation means were small relative to woody loads: 0.24–0.59 before PCT and 0.11–0.35 afterward, with broad relative uncertainty. title: Introduction
text:
Introduction
Developing and maintaining multiaged stand structures requires silvicultural systems that create and sustain cohorts of different ages within the same stand (O’Hara, 1998; Schütz, 2002). Retention systems can retain a range of tree densities in dispersed or aggregated patterns and can be used to maintain multiaged stands or transform formerly even-aged stands (Mitchell & Beese, 2002).
Coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) is well suited to this objective because it regenerates reliably by stump sprouting and can grow beneath a retained overstory. Its response to light is nevertheless important: reduced access to light can limit sprout vigor and persistence (Berrill et al., 2018; Muma et al., 2022; O’Hara et al., 2007). Tanoak (Notholithocarpus densiflorus) is also shade tolerant and a vigorous resprouter, making its response relevant to both stand development and management of competing vegetation (Berrill et al., 2021; O’Hara et al., 2017).
Silvicultural decisions that promote regeneration also influence the fuel conditions in which later management and fire occur. This paper therefore examines regeneration under varying overstory retention and describes surface fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning as reference information for integrated silvicultural, fuels, fire, and potential modeling applications.
We use 10-year measurements from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment to evaluate regeneration responses among retention treatments and to report fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including their PCT-associated contrast. Redwood and tanoak provide the primary regeneration focus, with other species retained as descriptive context where useful. Fuel components will be presented in a publication-specific form after their analytical specification is reviewed.
